text:
Somebody just automated the 6am version of you.

What changed: GitHub Copilot CLI shipped scheduled agent tasks this week -- hourly, daily, weekly, or on demand, running with no open laptop and no human at the keyboard.

What it actually does: it gives an agent a clock instead of a chat window. Define the job once -- check the inbox, flag what needs a reply, summarize what came in overnight -- and it runs on the schedule you set, not the schedule of when you happen to open the app.

Why builders should care: most people's AI use still starts with them typing a prompt. This flips it. The agent starts the work. You review the output. That is the difference between a chat habit and an actual system.

Try this this week: pick the one task you already do the exact same way every single morning. Write down its three steps. Hand those steps to a scheduled agent and let it run once before you touch your inbox.

The bigger signal: prompts were always the demo. Scheduling is the workflow. The tools are quietly moving from something you ask to something you run.

text:
Most people are trying to replace themselves with AI. Wrong move.

The real question is not who does this job. It's what are the actual tasks inside the role, and which ones are repeatable enough to hand off.

Here's a small framework we use before automating anything: List every task inside one role you fill. Sort by what repeats the same way every single time. Point AI at the smallest repeatable task first -- not the whole job.

Do this once and you stop managing headcount. You start designing systems.

Save this for your next build.
